questions.prompt: An applicant has W2 income of $120k, tax returns averaging $85k after depreciation and home-office deductions, and recent paystubs annualizing to $145k. Which prompt to AI is most consistent with the lesson's pattern?
choices: 'Given these three income figures, what qualifying income should I use?'
'Lay out each income signal in a table with source, period, gross figure, adjustments visible, and timing factors. Do not propose a qualifying figure or recommend which to weight.'
'The applicant's true income is probably somewhere between $85k and $145k. Help me pick a defensible midpoint.'
'Annualize the paystub and tell me if it is consistent with the W2 trend.'
questions.explanation: The lesson's pattern is: AI maps the signals, the underwriter decides the number. The first and third options ask the model to make a credit decision — what figure to use or what midpoint is defensible — which is exactly the line the lesson tells you not to cross. The fourth option asks the model for an assessment of consistency, which is also a judgment call dressed up as analysis. Only the second option keeps the model on synthesis.

questions.prompt: After the model lays out the three income signals in a clean table, it volunteers in the closing paragraph: 'A reasonable approach would be to use a blended figure of $115k as conservative qualifying income.' What is the right response?
choices: Use the $115k figure since it is the model's conservative blend and conservatism reduces risk
Remove the recommendation from the output, write your own reconciliation in your own words, and adjust your prompt next time to forbid recommendation
Treat the $115k as a sanity check against your own reconciliation and document agreement if your number is close
Use the $115k figure but require additional bank statement documentation to verify
questions.explanation: The model drifted into the recommendation space the lesson explicitly excludes — even though it sounds conservative, it is a credit decision the model has no basis to make. The third option is the trap: using model output as a 'sanity check' is how the model's framing quietly becomes your framing. Strip the recommendation, write your own number with your own reasoning, and tighten the prompt for next time.

questions.prompt: Of the four signals available — W2, tax returns with depreciation, recent paystubs, and 90-day bank statements — which carries the most weight for a working capital underwriting decision, and what is the right way to ask AI for help with it?
choices: Paystubs, because they are the most current; ask the model to annualize and project the trend
Tax returns, because they are filed under penalty of perjury; ask the model to confirm the return supports the request
Bank statements; ask the model to summarize total deposits per month and identify recurring versus non-recurring sources, without characterizing whether the deposit picture supports the application
W2, because it is the cleanest single-employer wage signal; ask the model to verify it is consistent with the other documents
questions.explanation: Bank statements typically carry the most signal for working capital underwriting because they show actual cash movement rather than a snapshot or self-reported figure. The framing of the AI ask matters as much as the choice of signal: summarize deposits, identify sources, do not characterize support for the application. The other options either pick a weaker signal (paystub spike, W2 from a side employer, returns that are already known to be heavily adjusted) or ask the model to make the supportability call. Both halves of the question matter.
